questions.prompt: The agent resolves 55% (target 80%). By category, it over-escalates standard photo-backed returns and tries to resolve policy exceptions on its own. An engineer suggests adding 15 few-shot examples of already-resolved complex cases so it 'resolves more'. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Define explicit escalation criteria and provide balanced few-shot examples showing both when to resolve (standard returns) and when to escalate (policy exceptions).
Add the 15 resolved complex-case examples so the agent gains confidence and resolves more cases on its own.
Have the agent score its confidence (1-10) and escalate below 7, calibrating the threshold with historical data.
Add sentiment analysis to avoid escalating when the customer is calm, reserving escalation for upset customers.

answer.text: Define explicit escalation criteria and provide balanced few-shot examples showing both when to resolve (standard returns) and when to escalate (policy exceptions).
answer.justification: The failure is a decision boundary miscalibrated in both directions, not a lack of capability: it over-escalates the easy and under-escalates what it should hand off. It is fixed with explicit escalation criteria and balanced few-shot examples showing both sides of the boundary. Adding only resolved complex-case examples biases the agent toward attempting policy exceptions; self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; and sentiment does not correlate with case complexity.

questions.prompt: Policy allows automatic refunds up to $500; above that it needs human approval and an auditable record. The rule is in the system prompt and in 2% of cases larger amounts were approved; compliance also wants an immutable log of every block. Which design reliably meets both requirements?

options.text: Reinforce the system prompt with the limit rule and ask the agent to record in the chat whenever it blocks a high refund.
A PreToolUse hook on process_refund that deterministically blocks amounts above $500, redirects them to human escalation, and writes the event to the audit log.
Add a max_amount field to the process_refund schema and trust the model to respect it.
A later step that reviews issued refunds each night and reverses those that exceeded the limit, logging the reversal.

answer.text: A PreToolUse hook on process_refund that deterministically blocks amounts above $500, redirects them to human escalation, and writes the event to the audit log.
answer.justification: The refund limit is a critical compliance rule and must be enforced in the middleware layer, not in the prompt. A PreToolUse hook blocks deterministically before touching the backend, redirects to human escalation, and can write the immutable audit log compliance requires. Prompt emphasis and the schema field depend on model compliance, and nightly reversal lets the improper refund happen and only corrects it late.

questions.prompt: An incident reveals that, during a 4-minute payment-gateway outage, the agent retried process_refund dozens of times and, once recovered, issued duplicate refunds; the tool always returns 'error' without distinguishing the type. Which change best prevents this incident?

options.text: Return structured errors with errorCategory (transient/validation/permission/business) and isRetryable, and apply bounded local recovery only to transient ones, treating already-initiated refunds as non-retryable by default.
Increase the maximum number of retries and add random jitter to space out the calls during gateway outages.
Catch the error and return an empty result marked as success so the agent does not retry.
Escalate to a human every time process_refund fails, regardless of the cause.

answer.text: Return structured errors with errorCategory (transient/validation/permission/business) and isRetryable, and apply bounded local recovery only to transient ones, treating already-initiated refunds as non-retryable by default.
answer.justification: The incident stems from indistinguishable errors: the agent did not know the failure was transient or that the operation might have started, so it retried blindly and duplicated refunds. Structured errors with category and isRetryable allow retrying only the transient ones and treating refunds as non-retryable unless confirmed. More retries worsen the problem, marking empty as success hides real failures, and escalating on any failure wastes recovery of benign transient errors.

questions.prompt: In a 30-turn chat about three orders, the agent mid-conversation confuses the agreed refund ($85) with another order's total ($120); the history is progressively summarized and the key data ended up in the middle. What is the most reliable way to prevent it?

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window so you do not have to summarize the history.
Increase the length of each progressive summary so it retains more detail from the intermediate turns.
Keep a persistent 'case facts' block (amounts, order IDs, statuses per order) injected into every prompt, outside the summarized history and placed at the start or end.
Ask the agent to re-read the entire conversation history before responding to recover the correct data.

answer.text: Keep a persistent 'case facts' block (amounts, order IDs, statuses per order) injected into every prompt, outside the summarized history and placed at the start or end.
answer.justification: The transactional values are lost by two combined effects: progressive summarization condenses them and 'lost in the middle' makes the model ignore what landed in the center of the history. A 'case facts' block with the exact per-order data, injected into every prompt and placed at the start or end, preserves them reliably. A bigger model does not avoid condensation, longer summaries still bury data in the middle, and re-reading the history is costly and unreliable.

A free-prose summary generated by the model at escalation time, prepended to the chat.
A link to the CRM with the customer's history for the operator to consult during the call.

answer.text: Generate a structured escalation package with customer_id, issue_summary, order_id, root_cause, actions_taken[], refund_amount, recommended_action, and escalation_reason.
answer.justification: The operator should not reconstruct the case from the chat; they need a structured, actionable summary. An escalation package with the key facts, what was already attempted, the recommended action, and the escalation reason lets them pick up immediately and satisfies the record compliance requires. The full transcript and the CRM link shift the work to the human, and a free-prose summary is less reliable and may omit the required escalation_reason.

questions.prompt: get_customer returns two same-name customers: one with an email whose domain matches the sender's company, and another with more recent activity. The customer requests a $300 refund. What should the agent do?

options.text: Pick the customer whose email domain matches the sender's company, as the strongest signal.
Pick the customer with the most recent account activity, since they are more likely to be the writer.
Process the refund on both accounts and tell the customer to confirm which was the correct one.
Ask the customer for an additional identifier (order number, last digits of the payment method, or postal code) to disambiguate before touching any account.

answer.text: Ask the customer for an additional identifier (order number, last digits of the payment method, or postal code) to disambiguate before touching any account.
answer.justification: With multiple matches and a financial operation involved, any heuristic -- email domain or recency -- can select the wrong account and execute an improper refund. The correct move is to ask for an additional identifier that verifies identity before acting. Choosing by domain or recency is guessing, and processing on both accounts violates privacy and may duplicate the refund.

questions.prompt: Each get_customer returns 45 fields (marketing, sessions, flags) of which the agent uses 5; in long conversations that pushes the context above 70% and responses degrade and cite the wrong orders. What is the best solution?

options.text: Trim (via a PostToolUse hook or a wrapper) the get_customer output to the 5 relevant fields before it accumulates in the context.
Switch to a model with a larger context window to absorb the 45 fields without degradation.
Automatically summarize the whole conversation whenever the context exceeds 80%.
Instruct the agent in the prompt to ignore the 40 fields it does not need.

answer.text: Trim (via a PostToolUse hook or a wrapper) the get_customer output to the 5 relevant fields before it accumulates in the context.
answer.justification: Tool results accumulate tokens disproportionate to their relevance, and here 40 useless fields per call saturate the context and cause context rot. Trimming the output to the needed fields before it accumulates attacks the direct cause. A bigger model only delays the problem, summarizing at 80% is already too late (the model is degraded and may hallucinate its own summary), and asking to 'ignore' in the prompt does not stop those tokens from occupying the context.

questions.prompt: Your agentic loop closes the turn upon detecting phrases like 'I've processed your refund' in the text; in production the agent sometimes says it while still planning (and the loop cuts before executing process_refund) or repeats it (and duplicates the action). How should the loop decide the turn is over?

options.text: Expand the list of completion phrases and require them to appear at the end of the message to reduce false positives.
Stop the loop when it reaches an iteration cap that guarantees the action has already executed.
Strictly evaluate stop_reason == 'end_turn' as the only completion signal, executing tools only when stop_reason == 'tool_use'.
Check whether the response contains assistant text instead of a tool call and, if so, end.

answer.text: Strictly evaluate stop_reason == 'end_turn' as the only completion signal, executing tools only when stop_reason == 'tool_use'.
answer.justification: Parsing natural language to decide termination is a leaky abstraction: brittle to wording variations and to the model mentioning an action before executing it. Control flow must rely on the server signal stop_reason: end_turn indicates the turn is over and tool_use indicates tools must be executed. Expanding the phrase list does not remove the fragility, the iteration cap is only a safety fallback, and the mere presence of text does not distinguish an intermediate turn from the final one.

scenario.title: Structured Data Extraction
scenario.body: You are building a structured data extraction system that processes unstructured documents (invoices, contracts, reports) and produces output validated against JSON schemas. You must handle varied formats, missing fields, and edge cases while maintaining reliability.

questions.prompt: Your invoice extractor asks in the prompt to 'return a JSON object with these fields' and, at temperature 0, 4% of responses carry prose before the JSON or trailing commas that break the parser in production. You need to guarantee always-parseable output conformant to your fields. What is the most reliable approach?

options.text: Add a post-processor that extracts the first {...} block from the response and strips trailing commas with regex.
Define an extraction tool whose input is a JSON schema and take the data from the response's tool_use block, eliminating syntax errors by construction.
Reinforce the prompt with 'RESPOND ONLY WITH JSON, NO ADDITIONAL TEXT' and several examples of the exact format.
Lower randomness further (top_p) and validate the JSON, retrying when parsing fails.

answer.text: Define an extraction tool whose input is a JSON schema and take the data from the response's tool_use block, eliminating syntax errors by construction.
answer.justification: tool_use with a JSON schema is the most reliable mechanism for schema-conformant output because the JSON is generated against the schema and syntax errors are eliminated by construction, taking the data from the tool_use block. Regex post-processing is brittle to variations, reinforcing the prompt still allows prose and trailing commas, and adjusting top_p with retries reduces frequency but does not guarantee valid JSON.

questions.prompt: After migrating to tool_use with a strict schema, the JSON is always syntactically valid, but accounting detects that in 6% of invoices the line_items do not add up to the total and sometimes the tax is in the subtotal field. What is the correct diagnosis and fix?

options.text: The schema guarantees shape but not semantics; you should extract stated_total and calculated_total, compare them, and on a discrepancy retry with the specific error or flag for review.
The schema is not strict enough; making subtotal, tax, and total required fields will force the model to reconcile them.
It is a model calculation problem; lowering the temperature and adding 'add carefully' to the prompt fixes it.
The source documents are poorly scanned; it is best to reject them and request better copies.

answer.text: The schema guarantees shape but not semantics; you should extract stated_total and calculated_total, compare them, and on a discrepancy retry with the specific error or flag for review.
answer.justification: A strict schema eliminates syntax errors but not semantic ones: it does not prevent amounts from not adding up or a value from landing in the wrong field. The solution is content validation -- extract stated_total and calculated_total, compare them, and retry with the specific error or route to review. More required fields do not force arithmetic consistency, temperature does not address semantic correctness, and blaming the scan ignores that the failure is in the extraction.

questions.prompt: You extract contract clauses with governing_law marked as required; when the contract sets no jurisdiction, the model fills in a plausible one ('State of Delaware') instead of leaving it empty, injecting false data. Adding 'do not invent absent data' was not enough. What is the best solution?

options.text: Make governing_law nullable/optional in the schema so the model can legitimately omit it when the document does not contain it.
Reinforce the 'do not invent absent data' instruction with few-shot examples of fields left blank.
A later validator that checks whether the jurisdiction appears verbatim in the text and, if not, clears the value.
Retry the contract extraction until the model returns the same value twice in a row.

answer.text: Make governing_law nullable/optional in the schema so the model can legitimately omit it when the document does not contain it.
answer.justification: Marking a field that may not exist as required pushes the model to fabricate a value to satisfy the schema. Making it nullable/optional lets it legitimately omit it when the document does not contain it, which is the root cause. The prompt instruction already failed and remains probabilistic, the later validator is a patch that does not prevent the initial fabrication, and retrying does not create information that is not in the contract.

questions.prompt: In a batch of 2,000 invoices, 180 fail validation: some due to locally formatted dates that do not match the pattern, others because the document does not include the order number the schema expects. An engineer proposes retrying all 180 with feedback. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Retry all 180 with error feedback, since appending the specific error lets the model correct any validation failure.
Flag all 180 for human review without retrying, because retries rarely help in extraction.
Distinguish the failure types: retry with feedback the ones failing on date format, and flag as missing (without retrying) the ones lacking the order number in the document.
Reprocess the whole batch with a stricter prompt about dates and order numbers.

answer.text: Distinguish the failure types: retry with feedback the ones failing on date format, and flag as missing (without retrying) the ones lacking the order number in the document.
answer.justification: Retry with feedback corrects format or structure errors -- like locally formatted dates that only need normalizing -- but is useless when the information simply is not in the document, like an absent order number. The correct move is to branch: retry the format ones with the specific error and flag as missing the ones that do not contain the data. Retrying all 180 wastes calls on the unrecoverable ones, flagging them all discards cheap corrections, and reprocessing the whole batch is costly and unnecessary.

questions.prompt: You classify documents into a 6-type enum; 9% fall into 'None of the above' due to unanticipated new types (credit notes, purchase orders) and 3% are illegible or ambiguous, and forcing the closest type already caused downstream errors. What is the best schema design?

options.text: Add an 'other' value with a text detail field for unanticipated types and an 'unclear' value for ambiguous or illegible documents.
Expand the enum now with credit notes and purchase orders, and repeat the expansion whenever a new type appears.
Always force the closest enum type and record confidence to review the low-confidence ones later.
Remove the enum and leave document_type as free text so the model writes whatever fits.

answer.text: Add an 'other' value with a text detail field for unanticipated types and an 'unclear' value for ambiguous or illegible documents.
answer.justification: An enum with 'other' + detail absorbs unanticipated types without fabricating an incorrect category, and 'unclear' explicitly captures the illegible or ambiguous, avoiding the downstream errors of forcing the closest type. Manually expanding the enum for each new type is endless maintenance, forcing the closest reintroduces misclassifications, and free text loses the structure and consistency the enum provides.

questions.prompt: You have two workloads: (1) validating the invoice at checkout in real time, with the customer waiting within seconds, and (2) a nightly reprocessing of 200,000 historical invoices. A manager wants to move both to the Message Batches API for the 50% savings. How do you evaluate it?

options.text: Move both to batch and poll for status, accepting the latency in exchange for the 50% savings.
Keep both on the synchronous API to avoid result correlation and ordering problems.
Only the nightly reprocessing goes to batch (it tolerates latency); the checkout validation stays on the synchronous API because it is blocking and latency-sensitive.
Move both to batch with a fallback to the synchronous API if the batch takes longer than expected.

answer.text: Only the nightly reprocessing goes to batch (it tolerates latency); the checkout validation stays on the synchronous API because it is blocking and latency-sensitive.
answer.justification: The Message Batches API saves 50% but can take up to 24 hours with no latency SLA, so it only fits non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads like the nightly reprocessing. The checkout validation is blocking -- the customer waits -- and must stay on the synchronous API. Moving both to batch breaks the real-time requirement, keeping everything synchronous gives up the savings where they do apply, and the fallback adds complexity without solving that batch does not guarantee latency.

questions.prompt: You extract data from highly disparate clinical reports (the dose appears in tables, in prose, or in footnotes); increasingly long instructions perform inconsistently across formats. What is the most effective technique?

options.text: Write an even more exhaustive specification describing every possible location of the dose across all known formats.
Add 2-4 few-shot examples showing correct dose extraction across varied formats (table, prose, footnote), teaching the criterion to generalize.
Fine-tune the model on thousands of labeled clinical reports so it learns all the formats.
Build a separate pipeline for each report format detected by rules.

answer.text: Add 2-4 few-shot examples showing correct dose extraction across varied formats (table, prose, footnote), teaching the criterion to generalize.
answer.justification: When detailed instructions give inconsistent results across varied formats, few-shot is the most effective technique: 2-4 examples showing correct extraction in different locations teach the underlying criterion and let the model generalize to new formats. A longer specification remains inconsistent, fine-tuning is costly and rigid (and outside the practical exam scope), and a per-format pipeline is brittle and does not scale to unforeseen variants.

questions.prompt: Your pipeline must run extract_metadata (type, date, issuer) before an enrichment step that depends on those metadata, but sometimes the model jumps to enrichment or responds with text. Which configuration guarantees extract_metadata runs first?

options.text: Use tool_choice 'auto' and describe in the prompt that extract_metadata must come first.
Use tool_choice 'any' so the model calls some tool at each step and trust it to pick the right order.
Merge extract_metadata and enrichment into a single tool so the order is irrelevant.
Force tool_choice to the specific tool ({'type':'tool','name':'extract_metadata'}) on the first call to guarantee it runs before enrichment.

answer.text: Force tool_choice to the specific tool ({'type':'tool','name':'extract_metadata'}) on the first call to guarantee it runs before enrichment.
answer.justification: When one step must run before another, forcing tool_choice to that specific tool on the first call deterministically guarantees extract_metadata runs first. 'auto' lets the model skip the step or return text, 'any' forces calling some tool but does not fix which one, and merging both tools blends responsibilities and loses the separation that makes enrichment dependent on already-validated metadata.

scenario.title: Structured Data Extraction
scenario.body: You are building a structured data extraction system that processes unstructured documents (invoices, contracts, reports) and produces output validated against JSON schemas. You must handle varied formats, missing fields, and edge cases while maintaining reliability.

questions.prompt: Your extractor reports 97% global accuracy over invoices, receipts, and contracts; a quick sample suggests contracts (8% of volume) perform far below average. Before reducing human review, what is the most prudent step?

options.text: Measure accuracy by document type and by field via stratified random sampling, since the global average can mask one type (contracts) with poor performance.
Automate everything above 90% model-self-reported confidence and review the rest.
Reduce human review uniformly across the three types, given the 97% global figure.
Trust the 97% global because it already exceeds the business threshold, and monitor complaints to detect problems.

answer.text: Measure accuracy by document type and by field via stratified random sampling, since the global average can mask one type (contracts) with poor performance.
answer.justification: An aggregate metric can mask poor performance in a subgroup -- here contracts -- so automating based on the global figure risks accepting erroneous extractions of that type. Stratified sampling by document type and field reveals where automating is safe and where it is not. Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, reducing review uniformly ignores the weak spot, and waiting for complaints detects the problem too late.
